items.title: Territorial Acknowledgement
notes: Councillor Freeman opened the meeting with the following Territorial Acknowledgement:

Today the agenda includes a recognition associated with City support to the Canadian armed forces through a forward-thinking human resources policy that facilitates the ability for City Staff who are also reservists to answer the call to serve Canadians domestically and abroad.
I would like to acknowledge the important role that Indigenous community members are serving and have served in the Canadian Armed Forces.

As outlined on the Indigenous Veterans website, “the story of Indigenous service is a proud one. While exact numbers are elusive, it has been estimated that more than 12,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit people served in the conflicts of the 20th century, with at least 500 of them sadly losing their lives.”

These determined individuals were often forced to overcome many challenges to serve in uniform, from learning a new language and adapting to cultural differences, to having to travel great distances from their remote communities just to enlist. The challenges they faced often extended to their post-service life. Many Indigenous war Veterans did not receive equal treatment compared to other Canadian Veterans.

Many Indigenous men brought valuable skills including: patience, stealth and marksmanship from well-honed traits for those who had come from communities where hunting was a cornerstone of daily life. These attributes helped many of these soldiers become successful snipers and reconnaissance scouts.

During the second world war Indigenous soldiers took on a unique role of "code talker” where sensitive radio messages were translated into Cree so they could not be understood if they were intercepted by the enemy.

Indigenous men and women have continued to proudly serve in uniform and have been deployed wherever they have been needed—from NATO duties in Europe during the Cold War to service with United Nations and other multinational peace support operations in dozens of countries around the world. In more recent years, many Indigenous Canadian Armed Forces members saw hazardous duty in Afghanistan.

Closer to home, Indigenous military personnel have filled a wide variety of roles, including serving with the Canadian Rangers. This group of army reservists is active predominantly in the North, as well as on remote stretches of our east and west coasts.

The Rangers use their intimate knowledge of the land there to help maintain a national military presence in these difficult-to-reach areas, monitoring the coastlines and assisting in local rescue operations.

This long tradition of military service is also commemorated with the National Aboriginal Veterans Monument in Ottawa. This deeply symbolic memorial features a large bronze eagle at its top, with four men and women from different Indigenous groups from across Canada immediately below. A wolf, bear, bison and caribou—powerful animals that represent "spiritual guides" which have long been seen by Indigenous cultures as important to military success—look out from each corner. Remembrance ceremonies are held at this special monument, including on Indigenous Veterans Day which is observed each year on November 8.

As an Honourary Lieutenant Colonel with 31 Combat Engineers, “the Elgins” I would like to acknowledge the contributions made to the Canadian Armed Forces by First Nations, Inuit and Metis community members.

items.title: Moment of Reflection
notes: Councillor Freeman provided Council with moments of reflection.
At the beginning of this Council meeting, we pause to think about the needs of our community. May we show wisdom and compassion in all our decisions.
Flags are half-masted at City facilities in honour of the passing of John Shortreed, who passed away on Wednesday, April 15th.
John was a former City of Waterloo Councillor that served four terms. He sat on the 1980, 1980-1982, 1985 and 1985-1988 terms.
John stayed involved and interested in municipal business in the years after retirement, often contributing as a delegation or offering his perspectives to Council.
Flags will remain at half-mast until Friday, April 24th at sunrise.

items.title: Councillor Roe – Heritage Helping Housing Motion
notes: Motion tabled April 20, 2026 for Council consideration April 27, 2026.
Motion:

WHEREAS Architectural Conservancy Ontario (ACO) is the province’s leading non-governmental organization dedicated to the conservation and reuse of Ontario’s built and cultural heritage; through education and advocacy ACO encourages the prevention and adaptive reuse of buildings and landscapes of architectural, historic and cultural significance;

WHEREAS ACO has emphasized that strong heritage protections are compatible with and supportive of efforts to address Ontario’s housing crisis, particularly through the retention, rehabilitation and repurposing of older building for new residential uses;

WHEREAS heritage buildings can help solve Ontario’s housing crisis by offering solutions that are affordable, equitable, sustainable and uniquely Canadian; including the repair and reuse of existing buildings which provides faster, cheaper and a more sustainable path to creating affordable housing and by enabling the delivery of homes faster than new construction while also supporting a stronger jobs market;

WHEREAS older and heritage buildings represent an important and often underutilized opportunity to create additional housing units, provided that appropriate financial incentives exist to support renovation and code- compliance upgrades;

WHEREAS ACO has proposed that the Province of Ontario implement a new housing-focused “Heritage Helping Housing Building Grant” of $10 million per year to encourage property owners and developers to rehabilitate and make adaptive reuse of heritage buildings that creates new housing units;

WHEREAS such a provincial grant program would support municipal housing objectives, help revitalize main streets, encourage private investment, reduce demolition waste, and strengthen the economic and cultural vitality of Ontario communities;

NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that this Council request the Mayor send a letter to the Hon. Doug Ford, Premier of Ontario, with copies to the Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing, The Hon. Rob Flack, the Minister of Finance, the Hon. Peter Bethlenfalvy, the Minister of Citizenship and Multiculturalism, the Hon. Graham McGregor and John Ecker, Chair, Ontario Heritage Trust, requesting that the Province of Ontario establish the Heritage Helping Housing Building Grant as proposed by the ACO, and that a copy of this resolution be circulated to local and area MPPs and heads of council.

items.title: New Business
notes: Councillor Bodaly wanted to highlight that the Clair Hills Community Association had a skate and their annual general meeting at the Waterloo Memorial Recreation Complex yesterday, April 19. He appreciates the hard work the Neighbourhoods team and dedicated volunteers do to put these events.

Councillor Freeman recognized the staff of the Elected Officials office for running the Community Day at Albert McCormick Community Centre yesterday as well. There were a lot of folks out to enjoy skating and the magician.
Councillor Freeman also wanted to recognize the Waterloo Library’s 150th Anniversary.
They held a great event on Saturday, April 18 and there were a lot of community members there to celebrate.

Councillor Wright noted that the Uptown Waterloo BIA held their annual general meeting last Wednesday, April 15. There are a number of businesses celebrating milestone anniversaries, and it’s encouraging to see that commitment to the Uptown core.

Councillor Roach wanted to acknowledge that the Waterloo Wolves U18 AAA team won the Ontario Championships and now they’re representing Waterloo in the National Championships, currently in the second period ahead of Halifax.
Councillor Freeman also wanted to celebrate how well Rangers are playing this year.

Mayor McCabe wanted to add a few more comments about the certificate the City received earlier this afternoon for the Reservist Policy. She thanked Commissioner Ron Ormson for his leadership and for modelling that type of leadership for staff at the City and for other employers across the Region.

Ron Ormson thanked Kathy Weidhaas and Michael Burzynski for their leadership on this policy. The City was recognized in 2007 for a military leave policy, but the updated version is more robust. Only about four cities across Canada have a similar policy.
Councillor Freeman noted that many reservists work in the community and that the individuals that were here today parade out of Waterloo on Parkside Drive.

motions.item_title: Councillor Wright – Supporting a Provincial Deposit-Return Program
motions.text: WHEREAS Ontario is one of Canada’s only provinces without a deposit- return program for non-alcoholic beverages; AND WHEREAS Ontario has the lowest beverage container recovery rate in Canada – at roughly 50%; AND WHEREAS an average of 80% of all empties return to Beer Stores each year, and the deposit return provides a consumer incentive to consciously recycle; AND WHEREAS the Ontario government proposed expanding the program to include non-alcoholic containers in 2023. THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council call on the Province of Ontario to immediately seek to implement a deposit-return program for non-alcoholic beverage containers; AND FURTHER THAT a copy of this motion be sent to the Hon. Doug Ford, Premier of Ontario; the Hon. Todd McCarthy, Minister of the Environment, Conservation, and Parks; MPP Peter Tabuns (NDP); MPP Mary-Margaret McMahon (Liberal); MPP Aislinn Clancy (Green Party); the Association of Municipalities of Ontario, and to local and area MPPs and heads of council.
